newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg holds its breath as Red River flood crests.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg holds its breath as Red River flood crests.

text.p: Winnipeg residents and emergency workers on Thursday braced themselves as the surging Red River neared its crest, hoping that the city's protective dike could withstand the rising flood waters.

"People are on edge now. You see it creeping higher and higher every day coming to work on the bus," Tammy Usipiuk said as she and co-workers returned from viewing water levels at the forks of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers.
The forks are at the centre of Winnipeg, Manitoba's capital and biggest city with 650,000 residents.
About 29,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans have been evacuated and four Canadians have died so far in the most extensive Red River flooding since 1852.

"We've dealt with river levels five feet (1.5 metres) lower. Once you're above that you're in unknown territory and while we're above that comfort level, we're going to be uncomfortable," Winnipeg City Commissioner Bill Carroll said.

About 8,800 Winnipeg residents have fled their homes as the rising river seeped through dikes shielding five city streets on Wednesday and inundated Canadian farmland covering an area twice the size of Hong Kong. The dikes were repaired and five military rapid response teams were deployed.

"We will deploy all the resources necessary," Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young told a news briefing. Some 7,900 soldiers will be deployed across Manitoba by Sunday, one day before the western edge of the Red River crests at Winnipeg's Achilles heal.
Manitoba's capital is protected by a 25-mile (40-km) dike southwest of the city that was completed on Wednesday.
"It's very surreal to see this mountain of rock rising on the horizon," evacuated farmer Ray Kabernick said. "We feel really confident being on the side of the dike that we're on."
But authorities were worried the hastily built dike may break under the pressure of the river, which has flooded 800 square miles (2,100 sq km) of Manitoba.

"We're in a good, solid holding pattern today," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said as the Red River rose to within an inch (2 cm) of its forecast peak downtown. "But the crest is not a one-day event. The peak will be with us for a week and then will recede slowly."

In the event the southwest dike breached, engineers said Red River headwaters might reach Winnipeg within six hours and could raise the river's crest another two feet (60 cm) above its forecast peak downtown within 40 hours.
But emergency officials said they would divert those waters into a 29-mile (47-km) ditch parting the rising "Red Sea."
The white-capping floodwaters have already overwhelmed the U.S. cities of Grand Forks and East Grand Forks and swallowed the Canadian town of Ste. Agathe, as well as hundreds of farmsteads.

"It's just discouraging when people spent countless hours putting up sand dikes and it doesn't work," Morris area reeve, or mayor, Herm Martens said. "We're cautiously optimistic we're seeing the light at the end of the tunnel."
The Canadian government advanced C$25 million (US8 million) in disaster funds on Thursday in what Manitoba Premier Gary Filmon called the "largest civil disaster this century."
"The total bill will be several times higher," he said.
Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said he phoned U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to suggest a binational flood agency.
